alternative: Keep the GC for lifetime and make release explicit for anything outside the heap: close()/dispose APIs (or Symbol.dispose) on sockets, files and WASM resources, and WeakRef/FinalizationRegistry only for caches and diagnostics under their documented non-determinism.
idiom_name: none - GC owns lifetime; explicit close/Symbol.dispose for external resources
implementation_notes: Objects are reclaimed by tracing; there is no per-object count user code owns, and the two reflective APIs are deliberately non-deterministic - MDN states that a conforming implementation is not required to call cleanup callbacks at all and that cleanup callbacks should not be used for essential program logic. What replaces the classic structure: ordinary references (the GC keeps a shared object alive as long as any reference exists), WeakRef for caches that must not keep their target alive, FinalizationRegistry only for diagnostics and best-effort cleanup, and an explicit close()/dispose protocol on objects that own something outside the JavaScript heap.
pitfalls: Cleanup callbacks may run long after the object became unreachable, out of order, or never (page shutdown, registry collected first); never gate locks, budgets or file deletion on them.
A held value that strongly references the registered target keeps the target alive forever - the registry intentionally holds the held value strongly.
WeakRef.deref() can return undefined after any turn of the event loop, even without explicit GC pressure; every use must handle the undefined case.
